# When Arithmetic Changes Phase

## A threshold model linking cyclotomic reciprocity and critical phenomena

Mathematics often advances in two tempos. For years, a subject may accumulate local results: a new correspondence here, a compatibility theorem there, a bridge between two languages somewhere else. Then the landscape seems to reorganize. Ideas that once looked isolated become parts of a single structure, and the new structure begins generating consequences of its own.

Physics has a vocabulary for changes of this kind. Water freezes, a magnet acquires a preferred direction, and a random network suddenly develops a giant connected component. Each event is a **phase transition**: gradual variation in a control parameter produces a qualitative change in collective behavior. The tempting question is whether mathematical coherence can be described in the same way.

That question is too broad to answer by metaphor alone. What should count as a connection? What quantity should measure coherence? Where should the threshold lie? A useful model must replace impressions with an exact arithmetic statistic. The simplest setting in which this can be done comes from cyclotomic number theory and the rank-one, or $GL(1)$, face of reciprocity.

The result is a clean mathematical phase diagram. For each cyclotomic conductor $n$, there is a canonical connection count equal to Euler’s totient $\varphi(n)$. At a prime conductor $p$, the count is exactly $p-1$. If the proposed critical count is $10{,}000$, then a prime conductor is in the active phase exactly when

$$
p>10{,}001.
$$

Above that boundary, the model’s coherence grows as the square root of the excess connection count. Below it, coherence vanishes. The arithmetic statements and the deductions inside the model are exact; the interpretation of $10{,}000$ as a scientifically meaningful threshold remains a hypothesis to be tested.

## From roots of unity to a connection count

Fix a positive integer $n$. A primitive $n$th root of unity is a complex number $\zeta_n$ satisfying $\zeta_n^n=1$ but no smaller positive power equation of that form. Adjoining $\zeta_n$ to the rational numbers produces the cyclotomic field

$$
K_n=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n).
$$

Its symmetries fixing $\mathbb{Q}$ form a finite Galois group. A symmetry is determined by sending $\zeta_n$ to another primitive $n$th root, so the group is naturally identified with the invertible residue classes modulo $n$:

$$
\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\cong (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}.
$$

Euler’s totient $\varphi(n)$ counts those invertible residue classes. Therefore the Galois group has $\varphi(n)$ elements.

The rank-one complex representations of this group are its characters, meaning homomorphisms

$$
\chi:\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\times}.
$$

A standard fact about finite abelian groups says that a finite abelian group and its complex character group have the same cardinality. This leads to the central definition of the model.

**Cyclotomic connection count.** For conductor $n$, define $E(n)$ to be the number of one-dimensional complex characters of $\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})$.

The **Cyclotomic Counting Theorem** states that, for every positive integer $n$,

$$
E(n)=\varphi(n).
$$

The proof is short but structurally important. Cyclotomic Galois theory identifies the symmetry group with $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, which has $\varphi(n)$ elements. Finite abelian duality then says that the character group has the same number of elements.

When $p$ is prime, every nonzero residue class modulo $p$ is invertible. Hence $\varphi(p)=p-1$, and the **Prime Connection Formula** becomes

$$
E(p)=p-1.
$$

This is the bridge that turns a phenomenological edge threshold into a sharp arithmetic condition.

## An order parameter for coherence

A phase-transition model needs an order parameter: a number that is zero in the disordered phase and positive in the ordered phase. Let $E$ denote the connection count, let the critical value be

$$
E_c=10{,}000,
$$

and let $\kappa\ge 0$ be a coupling parameter controlling the scale of coherence. Define the coherence order parameter by

$$
C_{\kappa}(E)=
\begin{cases}
0, & E\le E_c,\\[4pt]
\sqrt{\kappa}\,\sqrt{E-E_c}, & E>E_c.
\end{cases}
$$

This is a mean-field square-root law. It is continuous at the threshold, yet its slope becomes singular as the active side approaches $E_c$. In the language of critical phenomena, the order parameter has critical exponent $1/2$ because

$$
C_{\kappa}(E)\propto (E-E_c)^{1/2}
$$

for $E$ just above $E_c$.

The choice is deliberately simple. It does not claim that mathematical communities literally obey a thermodynamic equation. Instead, it asks a precise conditional question: if cyclotomic character counts serve as connections, and if coherence follows this square-root law with critical count $10{,}000$, what phase diagram follows?

## The shifted threshold

Insert the prime formula $E(p)=p-1$ into the activation condition $E(p)>10{,}000$. One obtains

$$
10{,}000<p-1.
$$

Because $p$ is an integer, this is equivalent to

$$
10{,}001<p.
$$

This one-unit shift is the model’s central arithmetic observation. The critical edge count and the critical conductor are not numerically identical because a prime conductor $p$ supplies $p-1$ characters, not $p$.

The **Prime Threshold Theorem** states: for every prime $p$, the cyclotomic connection count exceeds $10{,}000$ if and only if $p>10{,}001$.

The proof is simply the chain of equivalences

$$
E(p)>10{,}000
\iff p-1>10{,}000
\iff p>10{,}001.
$$

This gives both sides of the transition. If $p\le 10{,}001$ and $\kappa\ge 0$, then $E(p)\le10{,}000$, so

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))=0.
$$

If $p>10{,}001$ and $\kappa>0$, then $E(p)>10{,}000$, so both factors in the square-root formula are positive and

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))>0.
$$

Combining the two statements yields the **Complete Prime Phase Classification**: for $\kappa>0$ and prime $p$,

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\le10{,}001.
$$

Above the cutoff, the **Square-Root Scaling Theorem** gives the exact value

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))
=\sqrt{\kappa}\,\sqrt{E(p)-10{,}000}
=\sqrt{\kappa}\,\sqrt{p-10{,}001}.
$$

For example, $p=9973$ is prime and gives $E(p)=9972$, so it remains inactive. The integer $10{,}001$ itself is not prime, but that does not weaken the boundary statement: every prime below it is inactive, and every prime above it is active. The first active prime is $10{,}009$, for which $E(p)=10{,}008$. With $\kappa=1$, its coherence is

$$
C_1(E(10{,}009))=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

At $p=10{,}037$, the excess is $36$, so $C_1=6$. These examples display the nonlinear onset: quadrupling the excess count doubles the order parameter.

## What the model says—and what it does not

The model makes an exact conditional statement, not a historical discovery claim. Its connection count is the number of rank-one cyclotomic Galois characters. That is canonical arithmetic data, but it is not a count of papers, citations, conceptual implications, or collaborations. Likewise, the value $10{,}000$ is selected as a modeling threshold; it has not been estimated from observations of mathematical practice.

This distinction is a strength rather than an embarrassment. A speculative analogy becomes scientifically useful only when its assumptions are exposed. Here the arithmetic input, the transition law, and the interpretation are cleanly separated:

1. **Arithmetic layer:** $E(n)=\varphi(n)$, and $E(p)=p-1$ for primes.
2. **Phenomenological layer:** $C_{\kappa}(E)$ vanishes at or below $10{,}000$ and follows a square-root law above it.
3. **Interpretive layer:** $E(n)$ is treated as a proxy for cross-domain connectivity.

The first layer is a theorem of cyclotomic arithmetic. The second is the declared model. The third is a research hypothesis. Consequently, the sharp conductor cutoff is exact within the model, while any claim about real mathematical discovery requires independent data.

## Why this baseline matters

A good baseline is simple enough to refute. More realistic models can replace raw character counts with graphs whose vertices are arithmetic objects and whose edges record independently established compatibility results. One can then measure the density of the largest connected component, the mean degree, or the susceptibility—the expected increase in global coherence caused by one additional connection.

Higher-rank reciprocity offers the natural next arena. Rank-two automorphic representations and rank-two Galois representations could form the two sides of a bipartite compatibility graph. If a giant component emerges at a stable normalized mean degree, the percolation metaphor would gain empirical content. If no stable threshold appears, the simple phase-transition picture would need revision.

Composite conductors also enrich the story. For general $n$, the count is $\varphi(n)$ rather than $n-1$. Since the totient fluctuates with the prime factorization of $n$, nearby conductors can carry very different numbers of characters. A threshold based on $\varphi(n)$ may therefore be crossed in irregular clusters rather than at one monotone conductor boundary. Prime conductors are special precisely because their counting law is linear and yields a complete classification.

The critical exponent is another testable choice. The square-root exponent $1/2$ resembles mean-field symmetry breaking. A network-growth model may instead exhibit linear onset, exponent $1$, or a non-mean-field exponent. Distinguishing these possibilities requires arithmetic datasets and finite-size scaling, not rhetoric.

## A precise metaphor

The phrase “mathematics undergoes phase transitions” is evocative but vague. The cyclotomic model gives it a disciplined form. Choose a canonical family of connections. Count them exactly. Declare an order parameter and a critical law. Then derive the resulting arithmetic phase diagram without blurring assumptions and consequences.

For prime cyclotomic conductors, every step is transparent: $p$ produces $p-1$ characters; the active phase requires more than $10{,}000$ characters; therefore activation occurs exactly beyond conductor $10{,}001$; and coherence then grows like $\sqrt{p-10{,}001}$.

That does not prove that the history of number theory has changed phase, nor does it forecast when a future conceptual revolution will occur. It does something more modest and more useful: it converts a grand analogy into a falsifiable mathematical baseline. The next advance must either connect that baseline to measured arithmetic networks or show why a different statistic, threshold, or universality class describes the emergence of coherence better.

For a positive conductor $n$, let $K_n=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ be a cyclotomic field and define the connection count $E(n)$ as the number of one-dimensional complex representations of $\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})$. Cyclotomic Galois theory and finite abelian duality imply the exact identity $E(n)=\varphi(n)$, where $\varphi$ is Euler’s totient. In particular, $E(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$. We then fix the phenomenological critical count $E_c=10{,}000$ and define coherence by $C_{\kappa}(E)=0$ for $E\le E_c$ and $C_{\kappa}(E)=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E-E_c}$ for $E>E_c$, with coupling $\kappa\ge0$. For prime conductors, the model is active exactly when $p>10{,}001$; for $\kappa>0$, coherence vanishes exactly when $p\le10{,}001$; and above the cutoff it obeys the exact scaling law $C_{\kappa}(E(p))=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{p-10{,}001}$. The arithmetic count and all deductions within the model are exact. The choice of $10{,}000$ and the interpretation of character count as cross-domain connectivity are modeling assumptions, not empirical conclusions about the history of mathematics. The construction supplies a transparent null model for future studies of higher-rank compatibility graphs, empirically derived thresholds, and totient-driven activation patterns.

## 1. Introduction

The language of phase transitions offers a compelling way to describe the emergence of large-scale organization from many local interactions. In statistical mechanics, an order parameter vanishes in one regime and becomes nonzero after a control parameter crosses a critical value. In random graph theory, increasing the density of edges can create a giant connected component. These mechanisms suggest a mathematical question: can the coherence of a body of arithmetic knowledge be modeled by a transition driven by a growing family of connections?

A direct attempt encounters three ambiguities. First, the word “connection” requires a measurable definition. Second, “coherence” requires an order parameter. Third, a critical value must either be estimated from data or explicitly declared as a model parameter. Without these distinctions, phase-transition language remains metaphorical.

This paper isolates a tractable rank-one model in which the connection count is canonical. For the cyclotomic field $K_n=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$, one-dimensional complex representations of the Galois group form a finite character group. Their number is exactly Euler’s totient $\varphi(n)$. This family has a reciprocity interpretation: its characters are the rank-one Galois-side objects associated with the classical abelian correspondence. Regardless of interpretation, the count itself is an intrinsic invariant of the cyclotomic extension.

We feed that count into a prescribed mean-field coherence law. Given a critical count $E_c$ and a nonnegative coupling $\kappa$, define

$$
C_{\kappa,E_c}(E)=
\begin{cases}
0, & E\le E_c,\\[4pt]
\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E-E_c}, & E>E_c.
\end{cases}
$$

The present model sets $E_c=10{,}000$. At prime conductor $p$, the identity $E(p)=p-1$ converts the activation inequality $E(p)>10{,}000$ into $p>10{,}001$. Thus a selected threshold in connection space induces an exact and slightly shifted boundary in conductor space.

The purpose is not to claim that historical mathematical discovery has been shown to undergo a thermodynamic transition. The connection proxy does not count papers or documented conceptual dependencies, and the critical value has not been fitted to data. Rather, the model demonstrates how a precise arithmetic counting law can be coupled to a transition law while maintaining a strict boundary between theorem and interpretation.

The main results are:

1. For every positive integer $n$, the cyclotomic connection count equals $\varphi(n)$.
2. For every prime $p$, the count equals $p-1$.
3. The count exceeds $10{,}000$ if and only if $p>10{,}001$.
4. For positive coupling, prime-conductor coherence is zero if and only if $p\le10{,}001$.
5. Above the cutoff, coherence follows the exact square-root law $\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{p-10{,}001}$.

The organization is as follows. Section 2 reviews the arithmetic objects. Section 3 defines the order parameter. Section 4 proves the complete prime phase classification. Section 5 gives algorithms and examples. Sections 6 and 7 discuss interpretation, applications, limitations, and future work.

## 2. Arithmetic foundations

### 2.1. Cyclotomic fields

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\zeta_n$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity. Thus $\zeta_n^n=1$, while $\zeta_n^d\ne1$ for every positive $d<n$. The field

$$
K_n=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)
$$

is the $n$th cyclotomic field. It is a finite Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

Each rational-field automorphism of $K_n$ is determined by its action on $\zeta_n$. The image must again be a primitive $n$th root, hence has the form $\zeta_n^a$ where the residue class of $a$ is invertible modulo $n$. Conversely, every invertible residue class defines such an automorphism. Therefore

$$
\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}.
$$

The group is finite and abelian.

### 2.2. Euler’s totient

For $n\ge1$, Euler’s totient $\varphi(n)$ is the number of integers $a$ with $1\le a\le n$ and $\gcd(a,n)=1$. Equivalently,

$$
\varphi(n)=\left|(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\right|.
$$

If

$$
n=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q_j^{e_j}
$$

is the prime factorization of $n$, then

$$
\varphi(n)=n\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left(1-\frac{1}{q_j}\right)
=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q_j^{e_j-1}(q_j-1).
$$

For a prime $p$, this reduces to

$$
\varphi(p)=p-1.
$$

### 2.3. One-dimensional representations

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. A one-dimensional complex representation, or complex character, is a group homomorphism

$$
\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}.
$$

The set of all such characters forms the dual group $\widehat{G}$ under pointwise multiplication. The structure theorem for finite abelian groups implies

$$
|\widehat{G}|=|G|.
$$

Indeed, if $G$ is decomposed into cyclic factors, then each cyclic group of order $m$ has exactly $m$ complex characters, determined by the image of a generator among the $m$th roots of unity. Products of groups correspond to products of character groups, so cardinalities multiply.

### 2.4. The canonical connection statistic

**Definition 2.1 (Cyclotomic connection count).** For $n\ge1$, define

$$
E(n)=\left|\operatorname{Hom}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q}),\mathbb{C}^{\times}\right)\right|.
$$

The term “connection count” is an interpretive label for a canonical arithmetic cardinality. Mathematically, $E(n)$ is simply the number of complex characters of the cyclotomic Galois group.

**Theorem 2.2 (Cyclotomic counting theorem).** For every positive integer $n$,

$$
E(n)=\varphi(n).
$$

**Proof sketch.** The cyclotomic Galois isomorphism gives

$$
\left|\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\right|
=\left|(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\right|
=\varphi(n).
$$

The Galois group is finite abelian, so its complex character group has the same cardinality. By Definition 2.1, that cardinality is $E(n)$. Hence $E(n)=\varphi(n)$. $\square$

**Corollary 2.3 (Prime connection formula).** If $p$ is prime, then

$$
E(p)=p-1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Theorem 2.2 gives $E(p)=\varphi(p)$, and every nonzero residue modulo a prime is invertible, so $\varphi(p)=p-1$. $\square$

This corollary is the decisive simplification. On prime conductors, the arithmetic statistic is a strictly increasing affine function of the conductor.

## 3. The coherence model

### 3.1. Critical count and coupling

Fix the critical connection count

$$
E_c=10{,}000.
$$

This number is a selected model parameter. No empirical derivation is asserted. Let $\kappa\ge0$ be a coupling constant. The coupling changes the amplitude of coherence but not the location of the transition.

**Definition 3.1 (Square-root coherence order parameter).** For a real or integer connection count $E\ge0$, define

$$
C_{\kappa}(E)=
\begin{cases}
0, & E\le10{,}000,\\[4pt]
\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E-10{,}000}, & E>10{,}000.
\end{cases}
$$

For a cyclotomic conductor $n$, its modeled coherence is $C_{\kappa}(E(n))$.

The definition has four immediate properties.

**Lemma 3.2 (Subcritical vanishing).** If $\kappa\ge0$ and $E\le10{,}000$, then $C_{\kappa}(E)=0$.

**Proof sketch.** This is the first branch of Definition 3.1. $\square$

**Lemma 3.3 (Supercritical positivity).** If $\kappa>0$ and $E>10{,}000$, then $C_{\kappa}(E)>0$.

**Proof sketch.** Both $\sqrt{\kappa}$ and $\sqrt{E-10{,}000}$ are strictly positive because their arguments are positive. Their product is therefore positive. $\square$

**Lemma 3.4 (Exact supercritical scaling).** If $\kappa\ge0$ and $E>10{,}000$, then

$$
C_{\kappa}(E)=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E-10{,}000}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** This is the second branch of Definition 3.1. $\square$

**Lemma 3.5 (Continuity and critical exponent).** As a function of real $E\ge0$, $C_{\kappa}(E)$ is continuous at $E=10{,}000$. For $\kappa>0$ and $E>10{,}000$, it has the power-law form

$$
C_{\kappa}(E)=\sqrt{\kappa}(E-E_c)^{1/2},
$$

so its order-parameter critical exponent is $1/2$.

**Proof sketch.** The subcritical value at the boundary is zero. The right-hand limit is $\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E-E_c}\to0$ as $E\downarrow E_c$, matching that value. The displayed formula directly identifies the exponent. $\square$

The derivative on the active side is

$$
\frac{dC_{\kappa}}{dE}= rac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{2\sqrt{E-E_c}},
$$

which diverges as $E\downarrow E_c$ when $\kappa>0$. This sensitivity is a characteristic mean-field signature, although the discrete arithmetic input samples the curve only at integer counts.

## 4. Prime-conductor phase diagram

### 4.1. Translation of the threshold

**Theorem 4.1 (Prime threshold equivalence).** Let $p$ be prime. Then

$$
E(p)>10{,}000
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p>10{,}001.
$$

**Proof sketch.** By Corollary 2.3, $E(p)=p-1$. Therefore

$$
E(p)>10{,}000
\iff p-1>10{,}000.
$$

For integers, $p-1>10{,}000$ is equivalent to $p>10{,}001$. $\square$

The strict inequality matters. A count equal to $10{,}000$ belongs to the inactive branch. The formal conductor boundary is shifted upward by one because the prime connection formula subtracts one.

### 4.2. Inactive and active regimes

**Theorem 4.2 (Prime inactivity).** Let $\kappa\ge0$ and let $p$ be prime. If $p\le10{,}001$, then

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))=0.
$$

**Proof sketch.** From $p\le10{,}001$ and $E(p)=p-1$, one obtains $E(p)\le10{,}000$. Lemma 3.2 then gives the result. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Prime activation).** Let $\kappa>0$ and let $p$ be prime. If $p>10{,}001$, then

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))>0.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Theorem 4.1 gives $E(p)>10{,}000$. Lemma 3.3 applies because the coupling is positive. $\square$

The condition $\kappa>0$ in Theorem 4.3 is necessary. If $\kappa=0$, the square-root amplitude is zero even above the count threshold.

### 4.3. Complete classification

**Theorem 4.4 (Complete prime phase classification).** Let $\kappa>0$ and let $p$ be prime. Then

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\le10{,}001.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The reverse implication is Theorem 4.2. For the forward implication, suppose instead that $p>10{,}001$. Theorem 4.3 would give $C_{\kappa}(E(p))>0$, contradicting its vanishing. Therefore $p\le10{,}001$. $\square$

This theorem covers both sides of the phase boundary and establishes that no prime-conductor exceptions occur within the model.

### 4.4. Exact scaling above the cutoff

**Theorem 4.5 (Prime square-root scaling).** Let $\kappa\ge0$ and let $p$ be prime with $p>10{,}001$. Then

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))
=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{E(p)-10{,}000}
=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{p-10{,}001}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Theorem 4.1 places $E(p)$ above the critical count, so Lemma 3.4 gives the first equality. Substitution of $E(p)=p-1$ yields

$$
E(p)-10{,}000=(p-1)-10{,}000=p-10{,}001,
$$

which gives the second equality. $\square$

**Corollary 4.6 (Amplitude ratio).** Let $p$ and $q$ be primes greater than $10{,}001$, and let $\kappa>0$. Then

$$
\frac{C_{\kappa}(E(p))}{C_{\kappa}(E(q))}
=\sqrt{\frac{p-10{,}001}{q-10{,}001}}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Divide the two positive expressions supplied by Theorem 4.5 and cancel $\sqrt{\kappa}$. $\square$

The ratio is independent of the coupling. Thus the coupling controls overall scale, whereas the conductor excess controls relative coherence.

## 5. Algorithms and numerical illustrations

### 5.1. Computing the arithmetic statistic

For a general conductor $n$, $E(n)=\varphi(n)$ can be computed from the prime divisors of $n$. A direct sieve-like algorithm begins with $r=n$. For every distinct prime divisor $q$ of $n$, replace $r$ by $r-r/q$. The final result is $\varphi(n)$. Trial division requires $O(\sqrt n)$ arithmetic steps in the worst case and constant auxiliary space apart from integer storage. Faster factorization methods can replace trial division for large inputs.

For a prime conductor, no factorization is needed beyond primality certification: $E(p)=p-1$. Given a certified prime $p$, classifying its phase is therefore constant time in the arithmetic-operation model:

$$
\text{inactive if }p\le10{,}001,
\qquad
\text{active if }p>10{,}001.
$$

The bit complexity still reflects comparisons and arithmetic on $O(\log p)$-bit integers.

### 5.2. Representative prime conductors

These values illustrate square-root rather than linear growth.

### 5.3. Sensitivity to the coupling

At fixed active prime $p$, Theorem 4.5 gives

$$
C_{\kappa}(E(p))=\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{p-10{,}001}.
$$

Multiplying $\kappa$ by $4$ doubles coherence, while multiplying $\kappa$ by $9$ triples it. Changing $\kappa$ does not change which conductors are active as long as $\kappa>0$. At $\kappa=0$, however, the order parameter vanishes everywhere; this degenerate case is why complete classification assumes positive coupling.

### 5.4. Composite conductors

For composite $n$, activation is governed by

$$
\varphi(n)>10{,}000,
$$

not simply by $n>10{,}001$. The behavior need not be monotone in conductor. A prime near $n$ has totient near $n$, while an integer with many small prime factors has a much smaller ratio $\varphi(n)/n$:

$$
\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}=\prod_{q\mid n}\left(1-\frac1q\right).
$$

Consequently, composite conductors can remain inactive far beyond the prime cutoff. This is not a defect; it is a prediction of using the canonical character count rather than conductor size itself. The prime family is singled out because it yields an affine counting law and hence an exact monotone boundary.

## 6. Interpretation and applications

### 6.1. A three-layer model

The model should be read as three logically distinct layers.

**Arithmetic layer.** The identities $E(n)=\varphi(n)$ and $E(p)=p-1$ are exact consequences of cyclotomic Galois theory and finite abelian duality.

**Phenomenological layer.** The function $C_{\kappa}$ and the critical count $10{,}000$ define a square-root transition model. Once selected, they determine exact consequences.

**Interpretive layer.** Cyclotomic characters are treated as a proxy for connections relevant to arithmetic coherence. This interpretation motivates the model but is not established merely by the arithmetic identities.

Separating these layers prevents conditional conclusions from being mistaken for observations. The theorem “activation occurs exactly when $p>10{,}001$” is exact relative to the stated order parameter and threshold. The stronger sentence “number theory itself becomes coherent at that point” would require a validated empirical map from mathematical practice to this statistic.

### 6.2. Null model for arithmetic networks

The rank-one construction can serve as a null model for richer datasets. Suppose a dataset records compatibility relations between automorphic and Galois representations. One may compare an observed graph statistic with $E(n)=\varphi(n)$, asking whether character count predicts graph size, component formation, or susceptibility. Deviations would identify structure absent from the rank-one count.

The model also clarifies which quantities should be estimated. Instead of selecting $E_c$, one could vary a weighted edge count and seek a peak in susceptibility, defined as the expected change in the largest-component density caused by one additional edge. A reproducible peak would provide evidence for an effective threshold. Finite-size scaling could then test whether the order parameter behaves with exponent $1/2$, exponent $1$, or another value.

### 6.3. Algorithmic use

The formulas provide a simple benchmark for software that explores arithmetic phase models. Given $n$, compute $\varphi(n)$; compare it with $10{,}000$; and evaluate the order parameter. For prime inputs, classification reduces to one comparison after primality has been established. This makes the family useful for testing visualization, threshold detection, and parameter-sensitivity pipelines before applying them to higher-dimensional graph data.

### 6.4. Conceptual use

The construction illustrates a general design principle: a phenomenological threshold becomes mathematically informative when paired with a canonical counting law. If a family has statistic $E(x)$ and activation occurs at $E(x)>E_c$, then arithmetic information about $E(x)$ translates the abstract threshold into a classification of parameters $x$. Here the formula $E(p)=p-1$ produces a one-unit shift. Other families may produce nonlinear, clustered, or nonmonotone activation regions.

## 7. Limitations and future work

The principal limitation is interpretive. A complex character is a representation, not a documented conceptual link between two mathematical results. Counting characters measures the size of a canonical rank-one family, but it does not directly measure how researchers combine ideas. Any empirical study must define edges independently and justify their relation to arithmetic objects.

The second limitation is the selected threshold. The value $10{,}000$ is not inferred from susceptibility, historical data, or a probabilistic ensemble. The resulting cutoff $10{,}001$ is exact, but only conditional on that choice. A scientifically stronger model would derive an effective critical value from data and report uncertainty.

The third limitation is the mean-field law. The exponent $1/2$ is prescribed rather than measured. Real compatibility graphs may have correlations, arithmetic symmetries, and local constraints that place them outside mean-field behavior.

Several directions follow.

1. **Higher-rank Langlands percolation.** For fixed global field and bounded ramification, construct a bipartite graph of rank-two automorphic and Galois representations, with independently established local-global compatibility statements as edges. $$
\{n:\varphi(n)>T\}

for large thresholds $T$. Because $\varphi(n)$ fluctuates with factorization, activation may occur in clustered patterns, unlike the monotone prime-conductor classification.

5. **Robustness under alternative order parameters.** Replace the square-root law with linear onset, logistic smoothing, or regularly varying functions. Determine which aspects of the conductor classification depend only on monotonicity and which depend on the exponent.

6. **Finite-size scaling and uncertainty.** In observed compatibility graphs, report confidence intervals for thresholds and exponents, control for database growth, and distinguish true component formation from changes in curation practice.

C_{\kappa}(E(p))<C_{\kappa}(E(q)).

**Proof sketch.** Differentiate the power function on its positive domain. The first derivative is positive and the second is negative. $\square$

## 2. Arithmetic foundations

### 2.1. Cyclotomic fields

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\zeta_n$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity. Thus $\zeta_n^n=1$, while $\zeta_n^d\ne1$ for every positive $d<n$. The field

$$
K_n=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)
$$

is the $n$th cyclotomic field. It is a finite Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

Each rational-field automorphism of $K_n$ is determined by its action on $\zeta_n$. The image must again be a primitive $n$th root, hence has the form $\zeta_n^a$ where the residue class of $a$ is invertible modulo $n$. Conversely, every invertible residue class defines such an automorphism. Therefore

$$
\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}.
$$

The group is finite and abelian.

### 2.2. Euler’s totient

For $n\ge1$, Euler’s totient $\varphi(n)$ is the number of integers $a$ with $1\le a\le n$ and $\gcd(a,n)=1$. Equivalently,

$$
\varphi(n)=\left|(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\right|.
$$

If

$$
n=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q_j^{e_j}
$$

is the prime factorization of $n$, then

$$
\varphi(n)=n\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left(1-\frac{1}{q_j}\right)
=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q_j^{e_j-1}(q_j-1).
$$

For a prime $p$, this reduces to

$$
\varphi(p)=p-1.
$$

### 2.3. One-dimensional representations

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. A one-dimensional complex representation, or complex character, is a group homomorphism

$$
\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}.
$$

The set of all such characters forms the dual group $\widehat{G}$ under pointwise multiplication. The structure theorem for finite abelian groups implies

$$
|\widehat{G}|=|G|.
$$

Indeed, if $G$ is decomposed into cyclic factors, then each cyclic group of order $m$ has exactly $m$ complex characters, determined by the image of a generator among the $m$th roots of unity. Products of groups correspond to products of character groups, so cardinalities multiply.

### 2.4. The canonical connection statistic

**Definition 2.1 (Cyclotomic connection count).** For $n\ge1$, define

$$
E(n)=\left|\operatorname{Hom}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q}),\mathbb{C}^{\times}\right)\right|.
$$

The term “connection count” is an interpretive label for a canonical arithmetic cardinality. Mathematically, $E(n)$ is simply the number of complex characters of the cyclotomic Galois group.

**Theorem 2.2 (Cyclotomic counting theorem).** For every positive integer $n$,

$$
E(n)=\varphi(n).
$$

**Proof sketch.** The cyclotomic Galois isomorphism gives

$$
\left|\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb{Q})\right|
=\left|(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\right|
=\varphi(n).
$$

The Galois group is finite abelian, so its complex character group has the same cardinality. By Definition 2.1, that cardinality is $E(n)$. Hence $E(n)=\varphi(n)$. $\square$

**Corollary 2.3 (Prime connection formula).** If $p$ is prime, then

$$
E(p)=p-1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Theorem 2.2 gives $E(p)=\varphi(p)$, and every nonzero residue modulo a prime is invertible, so $\varphi(p)=p-1$. $\square$

This corollary is the decisive simplification. On prime conductors, the arithmetic statistic is a strictly increasing affine function of the conductor.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Iterable

CRITICAL_EDGES: int = 10_000
PRIME_CONDUCTOR_CUTOFF: int = 10_001


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Return whether n is prime using deterministic trial division."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n in (2, 3):
        return True
    if n % 2 == 0 or n % 3 == 0:
        return False
    divisor = 5
    while divisor <= isqrt(n):
        if n % divisor == 0 or n % (divisor + 2) == 0:
            return False
        divisor += 6
    return True


def euler_totient(n: int) -> int:
    """Compute Euler's totient phi(n) by trial-division factorization."""
    if n <= 0:
        raise ValueError("the conductor must be a positive integer")
    result = n
    remainder = n
    prime = 2
    while prime * prime <= remainder:
        if remainder % prime == 0:
            while remainder % prime == 0:
                remainder //= prime
            result -= result // prime
        prime = 3 if prime == 2 else prime + 2
    if remainder > 1:
        result -= result // remainder
    return result


def connection_count(conductor: int) -> int:

    if kappa < 0:

    return sqrt(kappa) * sqrt(edges - critical)

    rows: list[PhaseRecord] = []

# Computational evidence

The selected model consists of binary words with no adjacent `true` entries. Direct enumeration gives:

| depth `n` | admissible words | count | all binary words |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | empty word | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | `0`, `1` | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | `00`, `01`, `10` | 3 | 4 |
| 3 | `000`, `001`, `010`, `100`, `101` | 5 | 8 |
| 4 | obtained by prefixing `0` to the depth-3 words or `10` to the depth-2 words | 8 | 16 |
| 5 | same recursion | 13 | 32 |
| 6 | same recursion | 21 | 64 |
| 7 | same recursion | 34 | 128 |
| 8 | same recursion | 55 | 256 |

Thus the first counts are `1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55`, namely the shifted Fibonacci sequence (OEIS A000045 under the conventional indexing `0,1,1,2,3,…`).

## Counterexample hunt

The proposed strict sparsity inequality cannot hold at depths 0 or 1: the admissible language is then the full binary language. This is why the formal theorem assumes `2 ≤ n`. At depths 2 through 8 the counts above satisfy both
`2^(n/2) ≤ count` (natural-number division in the exponent) and `count < 2^n`.

The exact recurrence and inequalities are not justified by this table alone; they are proved for every natural depth in `Catalog/FractalTruth.lean`.

# Computational Evidence

## Scope

The principal claims are structural implications between abstract classes of decision problems and analytic inequalities derived from a finite fluctuation identity. They do not define an integer sequence or a parameterized finite search whose sampling could support the universal statements. Consequently, computation is used only for boundary-case diagnostics; the conclusions rest on the exact hypotheses stated in the accompanying results.

## Small-case calculations

The finite information-bearing object is a single Boolean memory. Its uniform distribution has two outcomes of weight `1/2`, while the erased distribution has weights `1` and `0`. The exact entropy calculations are

| distribution | weights | Shannon entropy |
|---|---:|---:|
| uniform bit | `1/2, 1/2` | `log 2` |
| erased bit | `1, 0` | `0` |

Thus one-bit erasure loses exactly `log 2` nats. At positive `k` and `T`, the resulting lower bound `k T log 2` is strictly positive. The zero-work boundary is therefore inconsistent with the stated finite Jarzynski condition, rather than an example violating the derived second-law inequality.

## OEIS search

No sequence arises from the abstract reduction, hierarchy-collapse, or finite one-bit thermodynamic statements, so an OEIS comparison is not applicable.

## Counterexample hunt

The assumptions were varied at their sharp boundaries:

| altered condition | consequence |
|---|---|
| omit the extended Church–Turing inclusion | physical realizability no longer implies machine-polynomial membership |
| omit reduction closure | an easy hard language need not transfer easiness to its source class |
| omit positive temperature or positive `k` | strict positivity of `k T log 2` is unavailable |
| omit the Jarzynski condition | no lower bound on expected work follows in this model |
| omit stable propagation of adjacent hierarchy equality | collapse at one pair of levels need not identify all higher levels |
| replace erasure by an injective operation | the one-bit logical-irreversibility conclusion does not apply |

These checks expose necessary boundaries rather than counterexamples to the guarded theorems. In particular, no claim is made that every polynomial-time computation erases information or that a complexity-class collapse by itself has a thermodynamic consequence.
